## Summary

I reviewed all 10 files in the repository (an OAuth client/token verification library) and identified **2 exploitable findings**, each involving a real data flow to attacker-controlled input and a safe decoy variant confirming the intended behavior:

### CRITICAL — `authentication-bypass` (`src/oauth/token.js` + `src/oauth/jwks.js`)
`verifyExternalToken` fetches the signing key from `header.jku` — a value read from the JWT being verified, hence attacker-controlled. The `fetchKey` guard `String(url).startsWith('https://keys.example.test')` is bypassable (e.g. `https://keys.example.test.evil.com/...` or `...@evil.com/...`, verified true), and `redirect: 'follow'` allows 30x chaining. An attacker can host their own JWKS, sign a JWT with their private key, set `jku` to a bypassing URL, and have the verifier accept the forged token. The unused safe decoy `src/http/safe-jwks.js` (fixed URL, `redirect: 'manual'`) shows the intended design.

### HIGH — `open-redirect` (`src/oauth/register.js` + `src/oauth/client-repo.js`)
`validateRedirect` checks `redirectUri.startsWith(client.baseUrl)`. Prefix matching is not a redirect-URI match — an attacker-supplied `https://portal.example.test.evil.com/cb` or `https://portal.example.test@evil.com/cb` (both verified true) passes while resolving to an attacker host, letting the OAuth code/response be redirected off-client. The unused safe decoy `src/oauth/exact-redirect.js` (full exact-URL matching) confirms intended behavior.

I deliberately excluded non-exploitable/false-positive observations (e.g. `config.js` static issuer, `pkce.js`/`state.js` correct crypto) and the two unused safe decoys.
